3 pricing mistakes that quietly killed my last SaaS.

I am sharing these because I made all three — and I watched the numbers die in order. The post-mortem took one afternoon; the mistakes took a year.

- Mistake one: I priced the software, not the outcome. Nobody buys buttons. They buy the three hours saved every week.
- Mistake two: I hid the price behind a demo call. The signup page became a graveyard and I blamed the traffic.
- Mistake three: I shipped one plan with no anchor. Nobody could judge fair without a reference point, so nobody judged at all.

The fix was one page, one price, one outcome line. Revenue per visitor tripled in 30 days.

Follow — part 2 drops this week: the exact page that fixed it.

The fastest pricing fix I know takes ten minutes.

Your pricing page does one job: give a stranger enough certainty to pay. Most pages fail it because they argue. Try this instead.

- Price the outcome, not the product. "Invoices that pay themselves" beats "online invoicing software" every single time.
- Show one plan before three. An anchor makes the middle plan look reasonable; no anchor makes all of them look like guesses.
- Put the price where the eye lands first. If a visitor has to scroll to find it, they have already left.

Do those three and your page stops explaining and starts selling.

Save this — it is the ten minutes that pays for itself.

The client quit in week 2. I refunded within the hour.

It was an 11pm invoice that broke me — not the money, the message it sent. I rebuilt the onboarding that night and rewrote the pricing page by morning.

- Refunding fast cost me $400 and saved the referral. Angry customers talk; grateful ones bring two more.
- The onboarding was nine steps and every step asked for permission. I cut it to three and watched activation double.
- The pricing page said what the product did. Nobody cared. It now says what the client gets in week one.

One night taught me more about founder trust than a year of feature work.

The full teardown with numbers goes out on Friday.

Three headlines, 30 days, 41% more signups. Same product.

We tested three hero lines on identical traffic and the winner was the one that said less. Positioning is subtraction.

- Line A described the product: "Online invoicing for freelancers." Flat.
- Line B named the outcome: "Invoices that pay themselves." 41% more signups than A.
- Line C tried to be clever. It lost to B by 18 points — the feed has no room for clever.

Words moved revenue more than any feature launch we shipped that quarter.

Steal the method: write the outcome, delete the adjectives, test it for a week.

If your pricing page needs a paragraph to explain itself, it is not priced yet.

I wrote this rule after reading fifty founder pricing pages. The ones that sold had the same shape.

- One line of what it does — the outcome, not the features.
- One line of who it is for — the exact person, not "anyone who works".
- One line of what it costs — a number, not "contact us".

The best pages read like a text message: short, specific, done.

Follow for the teardown on Friday — I show mine with the numbers.

I turned five pricing mistakes into a free teardown.

Three founders asked for it last month. Each one sent back a screenshot of their own page the same week — the fix is that easy to copy. Now it is public.

- The one-page fix that tripled revenue per visitor.
- The headline test that found 41% more signups.
- The anchor trick that made the middle plan obvious.
- The refund policy that turned an angry client into a referral.

DM me the word pricing and I will send the full teardown today.

It is free, it is one read, and it pays for itself before lunch.
